title: Lesson 8: Choosing What to Own: When a One-Off Is Better Than a Workflow
description: Choosing what to own: the discipline of deciding when a task deserves a workflow and when a one-off is the better choice, priced by build cost plus maintenance cost.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the full cost of a workflow that people most often forget to price in?
options: The maintenance cost, the recurring effort to keep the workflow working as inputs, tools, and the task itself change
The cost of the software license for the tool that runs the workflow
The one-time build cost of writing the template and setting up the connection
The cost of training a colleague to run the workflow for you
questions.explanation: The lesson says people price a workflow by its build cost, but the full cost is build plus maintenance, and the maintenance cost is the one that sneaks up on you: the recurring effort to keep it working as inputs, tools, and the task drift.

questions.question: According to the lesson, why is an unmaintained workflow worse than a one-off?
options: Because it looks permanent and reliable, so you trust it, and your trust rises while its accuracy falls as the world around it changes
Because a one-off always produces better output than a saved workflow
Because unmaintained workflows are automatically deleted by the tool
Because a one-off requires no review at all, while a workflow always needs one
questions.explanation: The lesson argues a one-off is honest about being temporary, while an unmaintained workflow looks reliable and you trust it, which is when it hurts you: the human is the last safeguard, and stopping the check removes the only thing keeping it safe.

questions.question: Priya runs the three-question test on two tasks. Which task should she leave as a one-off, and why?
options: The quarterly executive review deck, because its shape changes every quarter, so the frame is never stable and the setup is never repaid
The weekly team status rollup, because it is low-risk and therefore not worth owning
The quarterly executive review deck, because it is high-stakes and therefore too important to automate
The weekly team status rollup, because it recurs too often to maintain
questions.explanation: The lesson's worked example shows Priya owns the weekly rollup because it is the same shape every week, and leaves the quarterly deck as a one-off because its format, audience, and content change each quarter, so the frame is never stable and the build is never repaid.
